prompt: Phenoxide (PhO⁻) + allyl bromide can react at O (giving an ether) OR at the ortho/para ring carbon (C-alkylation via resonance). Which usually dominates in polar aprotic solvent?

options.label: O-alkylation — in polar aprotic (DMF, acetone), the charge sits concentrated on O, making it the main site of attack.
C-alkylation — the ortho/para ring carbons bear more HOMO density than O, so soft electrophiles like allyl bromide react there.
A roughly 50:50 mix of O- and C-alkylation — selectivity requires chiral catalysts to control.
No reaction — allyl bromide needs a transition-metal catalyst to couple with phenoxide.

explanation: Phenoxide is ambident. In polar aprotic solvents (DMF, acetone), the O is unsolvated and bears concentrated negative charge → it's the main nucleophilic site. In protic solvents (H₂O, EtOH), H-bonding to O 'hides' it, pushing the reaction to the softer C sites. Classic HSAB solvent-dependent ambident behavior.
